questions.question: In 2025-26, which area received the largest share of UK public spending on services?

options.A: Social protection (pensions, benefits and social care)

questions.why: Spending page: of every £100 spent on services, the largest share, £33, went on social protection. Health was next with £21.

evidence.text: the largest share, £33, went on social protection
Health was next with £21

questions.question: Which three taxes raised the most money in 2025-26?

options.A: Corporation Tax, Council Tax and fuel duties
options.B: VAT, Inheritance Tax and Capital Gains Tax
options.C: Income Tax, National Insurance and VAT
options.D: Council Tax, VAT and stamp duties

questions.why: Taxes page: Income Tax (£329bn), National Insurance (£204bn) and VAT (£180bn) raised 65% of all tax.

evidence.text: Three taxes raised 65% of all tax: Income Tax (£329bn), National Insurance (£204bn) and VAT (£180bn)

questions.question: The taxes page shows £134bn of borrowing in 2025-26. What is this borrowing?

options.A: A tax that most working people pay through their wages
options.B: The total the government still owes from all past years
options.C: Interest and dividends that the public sector receives each year
options.D: The gap between what was spent and what came in, which adds to the national debt

questions.why: Taxes page: borrowing is not income from tax; it is the gap between spending and receipts, and it adds to the national debt. Debt (the total owed) is a different number, £2,917bn.

evidence.text: Borrowing is not income from tax. It is the gap between spending
and it adds to the national debt

questions.question: In tax year 2023 to 2024, roughly what share of all Income Tax was paid by the top 1% of Income Tax payers?
questions.why: Who pays page: the top 1% of Income Tax payers owed 27.2% of all Income Tax. 59.1% is the top 10%.

evidence.text: the top 1% of Income Tax payers owed 27.2% of all Income Tax

questions.question: The site says taxes took 33.6% of gross household income in 2023/24. Which statement about that figure is correct?

options.A: It is an average across households, counting all taxes, and it is not the tax rate any one person pays
options.B: It is the Income Tax rate that most workers pay on their earnings
options.C: It is Income Tax's share of all the tax the government raised that year
options.D: Every household paid exactly 33.6% of its income in tax that year

questions.why: Tax and income page, 'Three numbers that are easy to mix up': 33.6% is an average across all people using their household's income and taxes. It is not the tax rate any one person pays, and it is not a share of all tax raised.

evidence.text: taxes took 33.6% of gross household income in 2023/24
It is not the tax rate any one person pays
That is an average across all people, not anyone's tax rate

questions.question: For people in the lowest-income fifth, which kind of tax makes up most of their household's tax?

options.B: Taxes on spending, such as VAT

questions.why: Tax and income page: for people in the lowest-income fifth, most of their household's tax is indirect (taxes on spending), 21.0% of gross household income.

evidence.text: For people in the lowest-income fifth, most is indirect

questions.question: The 'Tax and income' page shows an employee on £30,000 a year paying £4,879 in Income Tax and National Insurance. What is this?

options.A: The tax paid by a typical UK family, measured in an official survey
options.B: The average tax paid by UK workers, measured by HM Revenue and Customs
options.C: The measured tax bill of the middle UK worker in 2026
options.D: A made-up example that shows how the tax rules work, not a measured figure

questions.why: The example is headed 'Illustration, not a statistic'. The person is invented to show how the rules work, is not typical or average, and the result is not a measured figure.

evidence.text: Illustration, not a statistic
This person is invented to show how the rules work. They are not a typical or average person, and this is not a measured figure.
Together: £4,879

questions.question: After allowing for rising prices, how did the weekly pay of the middle full-time employee in April 2026 compare with April 2021?

options.D: The site has no figure for 2021

questions.why: Year by year, Earnings: £811 a week in April 2026 (ONS's provisional estimate), 4% more than April 2021 (£783 in April 2026 prices). Before allowing for prices it rose from £610, about a third, which is why A is wrong. Pay is compared from 2021 because the survey changed how it codes jobs in 2011 and 2021.

evidence.text: pay in April 2026 was 4% more than in April 2021

questions.question: Choose the year 2019. What was the average class size in state primary schools, and which part of the UK does that figure cover?
questions.why: Everyday life in 2019, Class sizes: 27.1 pupils in an English state primary school in January 2019; the figures are for England only. 21.7 is secondary.

evidence.text: the average class in an English state primary school had 27.1 pupils
England only. State-funded schools

questions.question: Compare 2015 with 2025. What does the site say about the change in the number of holiday visits abroad?

options.C: The two years are not compared, because the way it is measured changed
options.D: There are no holiday figures for 2015

questions.why: 2015 compared with 2025, Holidays: 'not comparable: definition changed (UK → GB)'. From 2024 the figures cover Great Britain residents with a new method.

evidence.text: not comparable: definition changed (UK → GB)

questions.question: In England, how did the share of households renting privately change between 2008-09 and 2024-25?

options.A: It fell from about 19% to about 14%
options.B: It rose from about 14% to about 19%
options.D: The site has no figures for renting

questions.why: Year by year, Housing: 19% of households in England rented privately in 2024-25, against 14% in 2008-09.

evidence.text: In 2024-25, 65% of households in England owned their home and 19% rented privately.
In 2008-09, 14% rented privately.

questions.question: Between 2015 and 2025 the employment rate for women aged 16 to 64 rose from 68.7% to 72.3%. What does the site say these figures tell you about why it rose?

options.A: It rose because of government policy
options.B: It rose because the economy grew
options.C: It rose because there were more part-time jobs
options.D: Nothing: the figures show what changed, not why

questions.why: Every year and comparison page says 'Change is not cause': the figures show what changed between years, not why, and they cannot separate the economy, prices, population and government policy.

evidence.text: Change is not cause. These figures show what changed between years. They do not show why.
Employment rate, women 16 to 64 68.7% 72.3% +3.6 percentage points
